## Block — Builderbot

> An orchestration layer that coordinates multiple AI agents across Block's entire codebase, invoked in Slack to take a ticket end-to-end to a reviewed PR.

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Year** | 2026 |
| **Status** | internal |
| **Domains** | coding, code-review |
| **Autonomy** | drafts-reviewed |
| **Headline metric** | ~1,500 PRs merged per week (~15% of all production code changes at Block) |

**Architecture**

- **Sandbox:** Not detailed publicly
- **Harness:** Agent orchestration layer coordinating multiple specialized agents; multi-player, real-time, operating inside Slack threads
- **Model:** Not specified
- **Tool Access:** MCP connects agents to internal tools and data; picks up Linear/Jira tickets, creates the branch, writes code, opens the PR, watches CI
- **Interfaces:** ['slack', 'linear', 'jira', 'github']
- **Knowledge:** Full-context index of Block's codebase — every service, API, and convention across hundreds of millions of lines and hundreds of services
- **Credentials:** Not detailed publicly

**Primitives**

- **Orchestration layer** — Coordinates multiple agents over one codebase instead of running a single loop
- **Ticket-driven flow** — Linear/Jira ticket → branch → code → PR → CI watch, end to end

**Key metrics**

- 200,000+ operations per day
- ~1,500 pull requests merged per week (~15% of all production code changes at Block)
- "What used to take months now takes days"

**Lessons learned**

- Concentrate investment on orchestration, context, and the environment — let engineers focus on the problems worth solving
- Meet people in Slack: tag @builderbot with a short description and it works in the thread
- Multi-player real-time collaboration lets humans steer research, planning, and implementation rather than only reviewing after the fact

## Brex — Internal Agent Platform

> Retool-based internal platform where employees build, test, and deploy agents for KYC, disputes, QA, collections, and operations.

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Year** | 2026 |
| **Status** | internal |
| **Domains** | finance-ops, support, customer-success |
| **Autonomy** | human-in-loop |
| **Headline metric** | 50%+ of support cases resolved by AI as first touch; disputes cut from 3h to 3s |

**Architecture**

- **Sandbox:** Retool-hosted runtime (no bespoke execution env described)
- **Harness:** Retool-based builder with prompt management and multi-model testing/evaluation; built by a ~25-person systems-engineering team
- **Model:** Multi-model
- **Tool Access:** An MCP server exposes external product features to the internal platform; new product tools become internally available immediately; invoked via Slack /c1
- **Interfaces:** ['slack', 'internal-retool-ui']
- **Knowledge:** SOPs uploaded as a knowledge base (e.g. 100+ page dispute guides); customer account data
- **Credentials:** SSO via internal Retool proxies (no per-user accounts); ConductorOne access management; Okta auth; data classified by risk; ≤30-day retention, no training on inputs

**Primitives**

- **Prompt + eval studio** — Non-technical ops staff design prompts, test across models, deploy with QA oversight
- **MCP tool bridge** — Product features exposed to internal agents through one MCP server

**Key metrics**

- 50%+ of customer-support cases resolved by chatbot as first touch
- Dispute processing: 3 hours → 3 seconds
- QA coverage 100% (previously sample-based); 1 person replaces ~5 QA specialists
- KYC adverse-media accuracy 85% → 88%

**Lessons learned**

- Target 40% automation, not 100% — the last mile drives investments that often yield zero value
- Treat internal ops with external rigor — build internal platforms to product quality
- Don't skip the human in the middle — end-to-end automation fails on accuracy
- Map workflows to the discrete steps a human would take, then translate each to LLM instructions
- Architecture beats vendor — legal/data approvals should follow data-handling characteristics, not the tool name

**Sources**

- [Agent, Human, Ops: How Brex Is Changing Roles and Workflows](https://www.firstround.com/reviews/agent-human-ops-how-brex-is-changing-roles-and-workflows) _(case-study)_

## Browserbase — bb

> One generalized agent in Slack that writes PRs, investigates sessions, queries the warehouse, logs feature requests, and runs browser agents across engineering, ops, sales, and support.

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Year** | 2026 |
| **Status** | internal |
| **Domains** | coding, code-review, support, customer-success, research |
| **Autonomy** | drafts-reviewed |
| **Headline metric** | Feature-request pipeline at 100% coverage with zero human effort |

**Architecture**

- **Sandbox:** Ephemeral Linux VM; pre-warmed snapshot rebuilt every 30 min; idles out after 30 min
- **Harness:** OpenCode core loop with 6 tools (read/write/edit/exec/safebash/skill)
- **Model:** Frontier models
- **Tool Access:** exec routes through a serverless integration proxy (Snowflake, HubSpot, Pylon, Grafana); the sandbox never sees real secrets
- **Interfaces:** ['slack', 'web-ui', 'webhook']
- **Knowledge:** Key repos cloned into /knowledge/; skills (markdown) loaded on demand
- **Credentials:** Credential brokering — the sandbox boots with references + rotating session tokens only; the proxy holds real creds; egress injection for a few hosts

**Primitives**

- **Skills (progressive disclosure)** — Markdown playbooks lazy-loaded per task so the general agent stays small
- **Integration proxy + RBAC/ABAC** — Scoped permissions per session make misbehavior structurally impossible
- **Credential brokering** — The sandbox runs arbitrary code yet never touches a secret

**Key metrics**

- Feature-request pipeline at 100% coverage, zero human effort
- 99% of first-response times < 24 hrs
- Session investigation: 30–60 min of log-diving → one Slack message

**Lessons learned**

- One agent with good abstractions beats a fleet of narrow bots
- Separate capabilities from the core loop — domain logic lives in skills + service packages
- Don't trust the model, remove its ability to do wrong: scope tools and services per invocation source
- Meet people where they are — Slack is the highest-leverage surface because that's where work already happens

**Sources**

- [How we build internal agents at Browserbase](https://browserbase.com/blog/internal-agents) _(blog)_

## Cloudflare — Internal AI engineering stack

> An internal platform of MCP servers, an access layer, and AI tooling (incl. an AI code reviewer) that makes agents useful inside Cloudflare.

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Year** | 2026 |
| **Status** | internal |
| **Domains** | coding, code-review |
| **Autonomy** | drafts-reviewed |
| **Headline metric** | 3,683 internal users (60% of company); 47.95M AI requests / month |

**Architecture**

- **Sandbox:** Dynamic Workers for sandboxed code execution; Sandbox SDK to clone/build/test
- **Harness:** OpenCode + Windsurf clients; Agents SDK (McpAgent + Durable Objects) for stateful sessions
- **Model:** Workers AI (open-weight, on-platform) + frontier models (Opus, GPT), routed by task
- **Tool Access:** MCP Server Portal — one OAuth point aggregating 182+ tools from 13 servers; AI Gateway for routing, cost, BYOK, ZDR
- **Interfaces:** ['cli', 'ci', 'web']
- **Knowledge:** Backstage catalog (2,055 services) + AGENTS.md generated across ~3,900 repos
- **Credentials:** Zero API keys on client machines — a Worker injects keys server-side; Cloudflare Access (Zero Trust) auth
- **Context Mgmt:** Code Mode collapses upstream tool schemas into search + execute, holding token overhead constant at scale

**Primitives**

- **MCP Server Portal** — One OAuth aggregation point for all MCP tools
- **Code Mode** — Collapse N tool schemas into 2 calls to hold token overhead constant at scale
- **AGENTS.md** — Structured, generated repo context (runtime, nav, conventions, boundaries, deps)
- **AI Code Reviewer** — Multi-agent CI review: risk tiering, specialist agents, Codex-rule citations

**Key metrics**

- 3,683 internal users (60% of company, 93% of R&D)
- 47.95M AI requests / month; 241.37B tokens via AI Gateway
- Merge-request rate ~doubled to 10,952 / week
- 295 teams using agentic AI tools

**Lessons learned**

- Centralize through a proxy early — direct-to-gateway looks simpler but blocks per-user attribution, model cataloging, and policy later
- Without structured data, agents are working blind — they read code but can't see the system around it (Backstage / AGENTS.md)
- Tool schemas eat context (34 GitLab tools ≈ 7.5% of a 200K window) — collapse them at the portal
- Frontier + open-source hybrid: route a growing share of workloads to cheaper self-hosted models

**Sources**

- [The AI engineering stack we built internally](https://blog.cloudflare.com/internal-ai-engineering-stack/) _(blog)_

> A cloud-based agents platform for engineers that delegates unattended engineering tasks to secure autonomous agents.

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Year** | 2026 |
| **Status** | internal |
| **Domains** | code-review, coding, ci-triage, on-call, maintenance |
| **Autonomy** | drafts-reviewed |
| **Headline metric** | 130,000 engineering tasks automated in one month |

**Architecture**

- **Sandbox:** Firecracker microVMs; <5s p95 end-to-end setup (boot, clone repos, install tools, configure harness)
- **Harness:** Supports multiple coding-agent harnesses behind a common interface
- **Model:** Multiple frontier models
- **Tool Access:** In-house MCP gateway ('Agent Gateway'); tools declared per playbook, permissions scoped per task, every action logged
- **Interfaces:** ['slack', 'github', 'cron', 'cli', 'conversational-skill']
- **Knowledge:** DoorDash-specific context packaged into playbooks
- **Credentials:** Scoped per playbook; brokered through the gateway, never on the laptop

**Primitives**

- **Sandbox** — Isolated Firecracker microVM with repos, tools, secrets, and runtime deps
- **MCP Gateway** — Governed, audited access to CI, observability, issue trackers, deploy, code search
- **Playbook** — YAML unit of agentic work: task, inputs, skills, tools, permissions, validation, outputs
- **Invocation Surface** — Trigger the same playbook from Slack, GitHub, cron, CLI, or a skill

**Key metrics**

- 130,000 engineering tasks automated in one month
- 25,000+ automated code reviews per week
- 300+ playbooks; 10,000+ invocations per week

**Lessons learned**

- Start narrow to earn trust — began with automated code review (frequent, measurable, easy to evaluate) before CI triage, on-call, maintenance, ticket-driven dev
- Make the work visible — public Slack threads drove adoption; private per-run channels did not build team habits
- Playbooks need enablement — workshops and hackathons turn repeated operational work into reusable playbooks

## Dropbox — Nova

> An internal platform for coding agents: engineers launch parallel sessions and internal systems invoke agents inside automated SDLC workflows.

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Year** | 2026 |
| **Status** | internal |
| **Domains** | coding, ci-triage, on-call, maintenance |
| **Autonomy** | human-in-loop |
| **Headline metric** | Dozens of agents in parallel from one runbook; migrations across thousands of entries |

**Architecture**

- **Sandbox:** Isolated env with a codebase snapshot at a specific commit; full Dropbox monorepo via Bazel; hermetic remote execution + caching
- **Harness:** Validation loop (propose → validate → feed back) with continue_on_validation_failure and max_iterations (~5); branch management kept outside the agent
- **Model:** Platform-agnostic — multiple coding agents behind one interface; swap models without rebuilding infra; prompt-eval tooling
- **Tool Access:** Skills/plugins to gather evidence, read logs, inspect failures; MCP integrations; Bazel-aware selectivity tools
- **Interfaces:** ['web-ui', 'cli', 'api', 'slack']
- **Knowledge:** Localized AGENTS.md per service; Dash (Dropbox context engineering); passing + failing test logs
- **Credentials:** Operates within Dropbox's existing infra and validation paths; same auth/authz as engineers
- **Context Mgmt:** Session history (notes/logs) carried across retry attempts

**Primitives**

- **Validation loop** — Bounded iteration with feedback on failure; deterministic systems control test execution
- **Dash** — Dropbox context-engineering system feeding agents across the SDLC

**Key metrics**

- Flaky-test remediation (Deflaker): 100+ validation runs
- Migrations applied across thousands of entries in parallel
- Dozens of agents launchable from one runbook

**Lessons learned**

- Platform value exceeds code generation — validation, guardrails, and context matter as much
- Context, validation, and guardrails reinforce each other to make background work trustworthy
- Not every step belongs in the agent loop — deterministic systems should control test execution and timing
- Integrate with existing engineering infrastructure rather than building separate AI-specific workflows

**Sources**

- [Introducing Nova, our internal platform for coding agents](https://dropbox.tech/machine-learning/introducing-nova-our-internal-platform-for-coding-agents) _(blog)_

| **Autonomy** | drafts-reviewed |
| **Headline metric** | Customer request → scoped issue → working PR, end to end |

**Architecture**

- **Sandbox:** Not detailed publicly
- **Harness:** Separate planning agent (issue creation) and coding agent (code generation); Code Intelligence for codebase knowledge
- **Model:** Codex used for PR review
- **Tool Access:** Triage Intelligence (auto-route, dedup, label); GitHub integration; testing Code Intelligence + custom MCP servers
- **Interfaces:** ['slack', 'intercom', 'linear-app', 'github']
- **Knowledge:** Full email/conversation context with metadata + attachments; Code Intelligence for decision history; Datadog/Sentry customer context

**Primitives**

**Lessons learned**

- Keep the agent close to the source of work (Intercom, Slack, Linear) — the best workflows live where work already happens
- Gradual autonomy — start by asking for suggestions, observe, add guidance, only automate once proven reliable
- Break work into small steps to keep coding agents focused and successful
- AI mistakes are useful — they surface failure modes to engineers
- Close the loop — auto-notify the customer when their request ships

## monday.com — Sphera / Atlas / Morphex

> An internal agent system on Amazon Bedrock where agents have identities, managers, scopes, and performance scores; Atlas ships features, Morphex ships PRs autonomously.

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Year** | 2026 |
| **Status** | internal |
| **Domains** | coding, code-review |
| **Autonomy** | autonomous |
| **Headline metric** | Morphex: 19 of 20 PRs merge without human review |

**Architecture**

- **Sandbox:** Amazon EKS, one pod per active session; a remote sandbox tests each PR before review; EFS workspace mount
- **Harness:** Claude Agent SDK behind a thin monday-agent-sdk wrapper (provider neutrality, cold-start optimization, custom harness opinions)
- **Model:** Amazon Bedrock; Application Inference Profiles for routing; cross-region failover; PrivateLink (traffic stays in VPC)
- **Tool Access:** Triggers via Slack @mention, monday item assignment, or GitHub PR review → SNS → per-team SQS → consumers; monday MCP servers underpin the Guardrails
- **Interfaces:** ['slack', 'monday', 'github']
- **Knowledge:** File-based memory: MEMORY.md (cross-session) + diary/YYYY-MM-DD.md; sessions/repos/secrets on EFS; durable records on S3
- **Credentials:** Per-session secrets in AWS Secrets Manager; same RBAC as humans; real Slack/GitHub/monday accounts
- **Context Mgmt:** Live state in ElastiCache (sub-ms); monday boards (Builders CoWORK) as shared state for tasks, status, handoffs

**Primitives**

- **Agent profiles** — Stable identity + assigned human manager + scope + performance score
- **PR Guardrails** — Automated review against monday standards (metrics, feature flags, security)
- **Memory as files** — MEMORY.md + daily diary instead of vector retrieval
- **Builders CoWORK** — monday boards as the shared-state layer for human/agent collaboration

**Key metrics**

- Morphex: 19 of 20 PRs merge automatically without human review
- 90% of engineers use AI coding tools monthly (up from ~50% YoY)
- Per-engineer PR throughput +50%
- Guardrails catches ~25% of agent PRs before human review; low single-digit revert rate

**Lessons learned**

- Evals from day one — should have been day one, not month nine
- Skip the vector store — file-based memory (MEMORY.md) was the right answer
- Remote-sandbox every PR before human review, with production-traffic replay
- The existing auth/identity/deploy pipeline applies to agents — reuse it
- AI engineering is building the feedback loops that let imperfect agents be trusted safely

**Sources**

- [AI Teammates: how monday.com runs production AI agents on Amazon Bedrock](https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/machine-learning/ai-teammates-how-monday-com-runs-production-ai-agents-on-amazon-bedrock/) _(case-study)_

## Ramp — Inspect

> A background coding agent that closes the loop on verifying its own work — runs tests, reviews telemetry, queries feature flags, visually verifies the frontend.

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Year** | 2026 |
| **Status** | internal |
| **Domains** | coding, code-review |
| **Autonomy** | drafts-reviewed |
| **Headline metric** | ~30% of merged PRs across frontend and backend written by Inspect |

**Architecture**

- **Sandbox:** Modal sandboxes; per-repo images rebuilt every 30 min from snapshots; warm-on-keystroke; a pool of warm sandboxes
- **Harness:** OpenCode (server-first) as the agent runtime; a plugin blocks writes until sync completes
- **Model:** All frontier models, MCPs, custom tools, skills
- **Tool Access:** Wired into Sentry, Datadog, LaunchDarkly, Braintrust, GitHub, Slack, Buildkite
- **Interfaces:** ['slack', 'web', 'chrome-extension', 'pull-request']
- **Knowledge:** Skills that encode how Ramp ships; repo images with the full dev env (Vite, Postgres, Temporal)
- **Credentials:** GitHub auth per user; the sandbox pushes the branch, an API opens the PR with the user's token (no self-approval)

**Primitives**

- **Modal sandbox + snapshots** — Pre-warmed full dev envs; fast cold start; effectively free to run
- **OpenCode runtime** — Server-first agent with a typed SDK + plugin system; code is its own source of truth
- **Multiplayer sessions** — Any number of people in one session; each change attributed to its author

**Key metrics**

- ~30% of merged PRs (frontend + backend) written by Inspect
- Session speed limited only by model-provider time-to-first-token

**Lessons learned**

- Own the tooling — it only has to work on your code, which lets you build something more powerful than off-the-shelf
- Work in public spaces to create virality loops; let the product do the talking, don't mandate
- Background agents that are fast are strictly better than local: same intelligence, more power, unlimited concurrency
- Move as much as possible into the image-build step so users never wait on setup

**Sources**

- [Why We Built Our Own Background Agent (Inspect)](https://builders.ramp.com/post/why-we-built-our-background-agent) _(blog)_

## Sentry — Junior

> An open-source Slack agent built at Sentry that acts like an intern — takes tasks, retrieves context, and is steered and reviewed by humans.

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Year** | 2025 |
| **Status** | open-sourced |
| **Domains** | coding, code-review, support |
| **Autonomy** | human-in-loop |
| **Headline metric** | Open-source Slack agent (~100k lines of TS) used internally at Sentry |

**Architecture**

- **Sandbox:** Vercel serverless functions; Vercel agent-browser sandbox with a MITM proxy for traffic interception; ephemeral containers
- **Harness:** Custom harness on Pi's SDK; a task broker over Vercel Queues with an inbox → worker-claim → interrupt/resume pattern to survive serverless timeouts
- **Model:** Claude Sonnet (faster); swappable (Opus as a more expensive option)
- **Tool Access:** Progressive discovery via MCP — by default Junior connects to no provider until the agent requests a tool lookup; a GitHub plugin with typed tools; Sentry CLI/API
- **Interfaces:** ['slack', 'web-dashboard', 'github']
- **Knowledge:** Conversation transcripts persisted in Redis; repo search to trace code paths; skill docs (TELEMETRY.md, SOUL.md)
- **Credentials:** MITM-proxy injection — the model never sees the token because it's never in the sandbox; plugins declare OAuth flows and credential domains; GitHub distinguishes read vs. write
- **Context Mgmt:** Incremental transcript updates in Redis; resource subscriptions to GitHub PR events for follow-ups

**Primitives**

- **Progressive tool discovery** — searchMcpTools loads tools on demand instead of dumping every schema into the prompt
- **MITM credential proxy** — Credentials injected host-side; the sandbox/model never touches a secret
- **Interrupt/resume broker** — Survives serverless timeouts via a queue + claim model

**Key metrics**

- ~100,000 lines of TypeScript (excluding tests)
- 4 months from start to writeup

**Lessons learned**

- Stateless compute fights you — serverless functions time out and disappear; model the agent around interrupt/resume
- Unit tests are the wrong yardstick for agents — invest in evals and integration tests instead
- Don't dump every tool schema into the prompt — progressive discovery keeps the context window lean
- Credential plumbing is real work — a MITM proxy keeps secrets out of the sandbox but adds significant surface
- Writes need per-user authorization, not blanket trust

**Sources**

- [Building an Intern (Junior at Sentry)](https://cra.mr/building-an-intern/) _(blog)_
- [getsentry/junior (open-source repo)](https://github.com/getsentry/junior) _(docs)_

## Shopify — Aquifer / River

> The Aquifer agent platform (session/harness/sandbox split) powers River, a Slack-native coding agent, plus research, migration, and app-security agents.

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Year** | 2026 |
| **Status** | internal |
| **Domains** | coding, code-review, research, security |
| **Autonomy** | drafts-reviewed |
| **Headline metric** | 1 in 8 merged PRs company-wide coauthored by River |

**Architecture**

- **Sandbox:** An execution environment (filesystem, shell, repo, build/test), separated from the harness — 'decouple brain from hands'
- **Harness:** Session (durable; Postgres append-only event log) + Harness (cheap agent loop) + Cell (ephemeral Go runtime); cells die, sessions persist
- **Model:** Swappable — the runtime is commoditizing; the value is in the harness + integrations
- **Tool Access:** Repo + tests + data warehouse + production traces + PR creation; a gateway credentials proxy
- **Interfaces:** ['slack', 'github']
- **Knowledge:** Monorepo 'World' (code + skills + conventions + intent docs + runbooks + AGENTS.md); Nix reproducible envs; Slack-transcript corpus mining
- **Credentials:** Gateway credentials proxy; per-profile sandbox policies; Shopify SSO
- **Context Mgmt:** Skills loaded on-demand as files, updatable per session; session survival across cell/sandbox/machine death

**Primitives**

- **Session/Harness/Sandbox split** — Durable identity, disposable loop, isolated execution — swap any layer independently
- **River (public-by-default)** — Slack-native coding agent in public channels only — visibility drives adoption
- **Skills as files** — Written-down knowledge mined from successful patterns and public transcripts

**Key metrics**

- River: 59,918 sessions / 30 days across 5,170 Slack channels
- 3,536 River-coauthored PRs merged; 1 in 8 merged PRs company-wide
- Median session 19 min; median 50 tool calls/session

**Lessons learned**

- Agent-friendly is human-friendly — monorepo, reproducible envs, written skills, and fast CI help both
- Local agents have a ceiling — private windows mean only the person at the keyboard learns anything
- Session survival is critical — cells die, sandboxes die, machines die; the conversation doesn't
- Treat agents as profiles, not platforms — a new agent is a new bundle on the same substrate

**Sources**

- [Under the River](https://shopify.engineering/under-the-river) _(blog)_

## Slack — Multi-agent context system

> A coordinator/dispatcher multi-agent design with structured context channels for long-running investigations spanning hundreds of steps.

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Year** | 2026 |
| **Status** | internal |
| **Domains** | research |
| **Autonomy** | human-in-loop |
| **Headline metric** | Megabyte-scale investigations without overflowing the context window |

**Architecture**

- **Sandbox:** n/a — this is a context-management pattern, not a full execution platform
- **Harness:** Coordinator/dispatcher: a central coordinator dispatches to expert agents and to critic agents
- **Model:** Not specified
- **Tool Access:** Expert agents produce reports; critic agents evaluate them using evidence-inspection tools
- **Context Mgmt:** Three channels — Director's Journal (working memory), Critic's Review (credibility-weighted findings), Critic's Timeline (deduped chronological synthesis)

**Primitives**

- **Director's Journal** — Structured working memory: findings, decisions, questions, hypotheses
- **Critic's Review** — A truth filter with credibility scores over submitted findings
- **Critic's Timeline** — A chronological, deduped, conflict-resolved synthesis retained across steps

**Key metrics**

- Handles multi-agent runs spanning hundreds of requests and megabytes of output

**Lessons learned**

- Don't pass all information at every step — build structured summaries agents can reliably build on
- Separate expert agents (produce) from critic agents (evaluate); corroborated findings are prioritized
- Context management becomes its own subsystem once runs get long

**Sources**

- [How Slack manages context in long-running multi-agent systems](https://www.infoq.com/news/2026/04/slack-agent-context-management/) _(blog)_

## Spotify — Honk / Xirp

> A background coding agent for large-scale changes (Honk) running on a vendor-neutral, model-agnostic session environment (Xirp) backed by org context (Portal/Backstage).

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Year** | 2025 |
| **Status** | commercialized |
| **Domains** | coding, migrations, code-review |
| **Autonomy** | drafts-reviewed |
| **Headline metric** | 1,500+ merged AI-generated PRs; ~50% of Spotify PRs automated |

**Architecture**

- **Sandbox:** Containerized runtime that runs transformations as jobs inside Fleet Management
- **Harness:** An internal CLI delegating to pluggable agents; Xirp coordinates 50+ parallel sessions, each in its own worktree, with the model swappable mid-task
- **Model:** Multiple and interchangeable (Claude Code, Gemini CLI, Codex, open-weight self-hosted)
- **Tool Access:** Local MCP for formatting/linting; an LLM-as-judge for diff evaluation; traces in MLflow
- **Interfaces:** ['slack', 'github', 'cli']
- **Knowledge:** Fleet Management for repo targeting + PR workflow; Portal/Backstage software catalog for ownership, deps, architecture
- **Credentials:** Inherits Fleet Management auth/authz for repo access and PR operations
- **Context Mgmt:** Xirp pairs with Portal: every session initializes with org context; transcripts/metadata flow back to Portal

**Primitives**

- **Pluggable harness** — Swap agents and LLMs without rebuilding the surrounding infra
- **Fleet management** — Target thousands of repos, run builds/tests, open and merge PRs at fleet scale
- **Org context (Portal/Backstage)** — Component architecture, dependency graphs, and ownership as a shared baseline

**Key metrics**

- 1,500+ merged AI-generated PRs (Honk)
- 60–90% time savings on migrations vs manual
- ~50% of Spotify PRs automated
- 36,000+ Xirp sessions; thousands of engineers

**Lessons learned**

- Flexibility is critical — a pluggable architecture enabled multiple LLM/agent swaps in a fast-moving landscape
- Migration and ad-hoc agent workflows share config improvements (symbiosis)
- AI lowers the barrier for changes that previously required AST/regex expertise
- Autonomy without structure fragments into per-engineer configs (CLAUDE.md, MCP setups) — shared org context is the multiplier

## WorkOS — Project Horizon

> An internal autonomous 'code factory' where a continuously running swarm of agents handles the implementation loop while engineers focus on requirements and acceptance testing.

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Year** | 2026 |
| **Status** | internal |
| **Domains** | coding, code-review |
| **Autonomy** | drafts-reviewed |
| **Headline metric** | A self-improving platform — every run ships work and feeds fixes back in |

**Architecture**

- **Sandbox:** Cloudflare Containers + Sandbox SDK; disposable, tightly scoped sandboxes with explicit lifecycle APIs and egress controls; full monorepo stack in Docker dev containers
- **Harness:** OpenCode preconfigured in the dev container; a worker processes webhooks; an agent orchestrator manages the sandbox lifecycle (create/pause/resume/destroy) and tracks state + artifacts
- **Model:** Not specified
- **Tool Access:** A custom MCP server stitches internal data sources (Datadog, Sentry, Slack, WorkOS Pipes); all outbound traffic proxied through Workers with allowlists, limits, logging, and token injection
- **Interfaces:** ['linear', 'github', 'slack', 'web']
- **Knowledge:** AGENTS.md and CLAUDE.md capture scripts, docs, conventions; MCP codifies the patterns engineers already follow; Notion + Figma for specs/mockups
- **Credentials:** WorkOS Pipes (no OAuth/token-refresh to maintain); scoped short-lived GitHub tokens per user; engineers use their own identity in the MCP; least-privilege + egress controls
- **Context Mgmt:** The orchestrator pauses/resumes sandboxes and tracks state + artifacts across a run

**Primitives**

- **Sandbox = execution primitive vs orchestrator = control plane** — Separate what runs code from what manages the lifecycle
- **Purpose-built agent infra** — A runtime controlled end-to-end, with lifecycle APIs and egress controls for the threat model
- **Self-improvement loop** — Each run ships work and produces the next set of fixes, surfacing where the platform is brittle
- **MCP as an iterative product** — Tuning tools is ongoing, not a one-time integration

**Lessons learned**

- You need purpose-built agent infrastructure — a runtime you control end-to-end with lifecycle APIs and egress controls
- Separate concerns: sandboxes are an execution primitive; the orchestrator is the control plane
- Make autonomy a platform — the system gets faster and more reliable through use as fixes feed back in
- MCP tuning is an iterative product, not a one-time integration — codify the patterns engineers already follow
- Build modularly so components can be swapped as tooling evolves

**Sources**

- [Project Horizon — an autonomous code factory at WorkOS](https://workos.com/blog/project-horizon) _(blog)_
